problem: Dense semantic maps are costly to maintain and adapt poorly to dynamic indoor scenes; navigation lacks mechanisms to assess and revisit semantically relevant places, causing redundant exploration; and environment changes degrade semantic anchors without incremental update or self-evolution.
motivation: Embodied agents in indoor digital-twin systems need efficient, long-term consistent exploration in dynamic, unstructured environments. Dense maps and static memory cannot handle changes and waste exploration resources.
key_idea: Replace dense maps with a sparse multi-scale semantic map plus an LLM-maintained area-object-feature memory network that is self-evolved by marking inactive objects on navigation failure and refining search strategies via a memory LLM (MemoLLM).
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited. The claim is that sparse semantic modeling combined with revisitable memory and failure-driven memory updating reduces computation and redundant exploration while staying consistent in dynamic scenes.
method: Sparse semantic mapping: multi-scale structured environment modeling without dense maps, lowering computational cost.
Memory-intelligence system: large-model-driven 'area-object-feature' relational network for semantic reasoning and revisiting relevant places.
Semantic relevance assessment and revisiting: mechanism to evaluate and return to relevant areas to avoid redundant exploration.
Perceptual-memory self-evolution: marks objects inactive when navigation fails.
MemoLLM: memory LLM that generates and iteratively refines candidate search strategies to dynamically update memory.
